strengths: Addresses a practically important and high-stakes NLP task: assisting authors with evidence-grounded rebuttal writing.
Proposes a clear multi-agent pipeline with explicit intermediate artifacts: atomic concern extraction, hybrid context construction, external evidence retrieval, response planning, and drafting.
Builds RebuttalBench from real OpenReview/Re2 data and introduces a multi-dimensional rubric covering coverage, argumentation quality, and communication quality.
Reports matched-backbone comparisons across four strong LLMs and includes ablations isolating input structuring, evidence construction, and checkers.
Provides detailed prompt templates and states that code will be released, which supports reproducibility.
Case studies qualitatively illustrate how the system surfaces intermediate planning artifacts and separates interpretive defense from required action items.
weaknesses: The core evaluation relies entirely on an unvalidated LLM-as-judge; no human agreement, reliability analysis, or judge-bias assessment is reported, so claims of improved coverage, faithfulness, and coherence rest on unverified judge scores.

The benchmark's observable post-rebuttal signal (reviewer follow-up reactions) is used for filtering/labeling but not to evaluate generated rebuttals; final evaluation still uses an LLM judge, undermining the author-centric/outcome-grounded claim.

Data construction is inconsistently described: one section says positive/negative labels come from reviewer follow-up comments, while the appendix says they come from final score/acceptance changes; benchmark size, exact splits, and selection criteria remain unclear.

The human-in-the-loop component is central to the proposed framework but is not evaluated; main experiments are fully automated, and no token, latency, or cost comparison against direct-to-text baselines is provided.

Metrics do not directly measure faithfulness to the manuscript or global consistency across responses, despite these being key stated claims; external evidence correctness and hallucination risk are not systematically checked.
No statistical significance tests or variance estimates are reported for the main improvements, and potential judge self-preference is not controlled.
The paper does not compare against prior specialized multi-agent peer-review/rebuttal systems, limiting evidence for the claimed superiority of the proposed architecture.

Several clarity issues remain, including naming inconsistency between RebuttalAgent and RESPONSEAGENT, 'first multi-agents framework' phrasing, and the unclear phrase 'top 20 papers with over 100 reviewers'.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and high-stakes task (author rebuttal writing) and reframes it as an evidence-centric planning/organization problem rather than free-form text generation.

The proposed RebuttalAgent pipeline is clearly described, with a detailed multi-agent architecture, intermediate artifacts (concern sets, evidence bundles, response plans), and an ablation study that isolates major components.

The paper introduces RebuttalBench and an evaluation rubric targeting relevance, argumentation quality, and communication quality beyond surface fluency; the benchmark is derived from real OpenReview data, and prompt templates are documented in the appendix.
The experiments show consistent improvements over same-backbone direct-to-text baselines across four LLM backbones, and the paper is generally well written and easy to follow.
weaknesses: The evaluation relies entirely on an LLM-as-judge rubric (Gemini-3-Flash) without human validation or correlation with human judgments. This is especially problematic because Gemini-3-Flash is also one of the baseline generators, raising self-preference/bias concerns, and no direct factuality or faithfulness check is performed.

There is a serious internal contradiction and ethical/methodological risk: Appendix D's Rebuttal Letter Writer prompt instructs the model to 'invent plausible, realistic values/results' and append an asterisk, which conflicts with the main paper's claim that the system inhibits result generation and prevents hallucination. This undermines the central faithfulness/transparency claim.

Benchmark validity and contamination are not addressed: the data come from ICLR 2023 OpenReview/Re^2, which is public and likely present in LLM pretraining; the positive/negative follow-up labels are not used for the main evaluation; and the exact test-set size is unclear (20 papers vs. 9.3K pairs), with no statistical significance or variance reported.

The baselines are limited to direct-to-text prompting with the same backbone. The paper does not compare against stronger or more relevant alternatives such as retrieval-augmented generation, self-refine, chain-of-thought, multi-agent debate, or prior rebuttal-generation systems.

Claims about transparency, author control, and human-in-the-loop benefits are not empirically evaluated: all main experiments run in fully automated mode, and no user study or author-facing evaluation is conducted.

Reproducibility is incomplete: proprietary model versions and the LLM judge may change, code is not yet released, exact filtering/splitting protocols for RebuttalBench are underspecified, and no seeds or confidence intervals are reported.
Minor presentation issues remain, including inconsistent naming (e.g., RESPONSEAGENT vs. REBUTTALAGENT) and several typos.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-explored and practically important problem: assisting authors in writing evidence-grounded rebuttals, which sits squarely within NLP/CL for scientific communication.

The 'verify-then-write' system design is well-motivated and clearly described: decomposing reviews into atomic concerns, constructing hybrid internal/external evidence, and separating interpretative defense from necessary intervention is a sensible response to hallucination in direct-to-text generation.

The evaluation rubric is thoughtfully designed and grounded in an empirical analysis of actual reviewer language (word clouds/histograms), and covers multiple dimensions (relevance, argumentation, communication) rather than surface fluency alone.

The ablation study (Table 2) is informative, isolating the contribution of input structuring, evidence construction, and checkers, and correctly identifies external evidence briefs as the most critical component.
Figures (1-2) communicate the pipeline and the contrast to prior paradigms effectively.
weaknesses: The entire empirical case rests on a single LLM-as-judge (Gemini-3-Flash) scoring 20 papers, with no human evaluation, no inter-annotator agreement, no validation of the judge against human judgment, and no significance testing or variance reporting. For a task whose whole purpose is to persuade human reviewers, and whose headline claims are about 'faithfulness,' 'traceability,' and 'verifiable grounding,' an LLM judge is particularly inadequate and potentially circular (a judge scoring the very kinds of evidence-grounded text the system was engineered to produce).

The paper's central contribution — transparency, verifiable grounding, and human-in-the-loop control — is never actually evaluated. All main experiments run RebuttalAgent in fully automated mode (explicitly excluding the human checkpoints), so the properties that distinguish it from prior work are asserted rather than measured. There is no evaluation of concern-extraction accuracy, evidence correctness, or whether the 'plan' actually reduces hallucination/over-commitment.

The manuscript is internally inconsistent in naming: the title says 'Paper2Rebuttal,' the abstract/system is 'RebuttalAgent,' and the conclusion proposes 'RESPONSEAGENT.' This strongly suggests hasty preparation and undermines confidence in the paper's care.

Numerical claims in the text do not match the tables (e.g., Gemini-3-Flash margin stated as '+0.33' but Table 1 shows +0.41; GPT5-mini stated as '+0.55' vs +0.57), raising concerns about the reliability of the reported analysis.

Serious research-integrity concern: the 'Rebuttal Letter Writer' prompt (Appendix D) explicitly instructs the model to 'invent plausible, realistic values/results' for experiments, using an asterisk to flag them. Fabricating experimental numbers in a rebuttal is precisely the misconduct reviewers are trained to detect; the paper neither problematizes this nor discusses any ethical safeguards, and the claim that asterisks 'prevent fabrication' is unconvincing.

The benchmark construction and its use are disconnected. The positive/negative partition is derived from reviewers' follow-up reactions, but this signal is never used in the main evaluation; the reported metrics come solely from the LLM rubric, so the carefully described 'decisive classification signal' does little work. The Challenge set of only 20 papers is also too small to support robust conclusions.

Possible judge bias: Gemini-3-Flash is used as the judge while Gemini-3-Flash is also one of the backbones under evaluation, and structured, sectioned outputs (which RebuttalAgent produces by design) are known to be favored by LLM judges. Neither self-preference nor format bias is controlled or discussed.

The 'first multi-agent framework' for rebuttal is overstated, given the cited prior multi-agent/simulation work (Yu et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2025b), and the claimed novelty is largely an incremental composition of known techniques (RAG, planning, multi-agent roles, checkers).

Reproducibility is limited: code is only promised, the corpus filtering relies on subjective LLM-confidence thresholds and manual curation of 'high-quality' dyads, and the exact judge/backbone configurations (especially the very recent GPT-5-mini, Gemini-3-Flash, Grok-4.1, DeepSeekV3.2) raise contamination concerns against ICLR-2023-derived data.

strengths: The paper reframes rebuttal assistance as an evidence-centric decision and organization problem, which is a sensible and well-motivated formulation beyond direct text generation.

The proposed RebuttalAgent pipeline is clear: atomic concern extraction, hybrid internal manuscript context, on-demand external evidence construction, planning/checkers, and optional human-in-the-loop refinement. The appendix provides prompt templates that support transparency and partial reproducibility.

The paper includes a substantial empirical effort: a new RebuttalBench corpus, a multidimensional rubric-based evaluation, multiple baselines on matched backbones, component ablations, case studies, and an author-centric human preference study.

The results consistently show gains across relevance, argumentation, and communication dimensions over direct-to-text baselines, with especially clear benefits on evidence construction and concern coverage.
The limitations, ethical considerations, and deployment risks are discussed constructively, which is a strength for a submission about a high-stakes academic workflow.
weaknesses: The benchmark ground truth is not fully convincing: the main text emphasizes reviewer follow-up reactions as labels, while the appendix describes outcome-based classification using score/acceptance changes plus confidence tiers, creating ambiguity about what the actual labels are and how reliable they are.

The evaluation is driven by an LLM-as-judge rubric with only moderate human validation (Kendall τ = 0.646 on 9 authors / 33 samples). There are no variance estimates, significance tests, or inter-annotator agreement statistics, and the claimed 100% annotation accuracy risks being circular or overfit to a small subset.

The paper does not include a compute-matched comparison. RebuttalAgent likely uses more LLM calls and external retrieval than direct-to-text baselines, but cost, latency, and token usage are not reported, so it is unclear how much of the gain is due to structure versus additional inference budget.

Reproducibility is limited: the Project Page and HF Demo fields are blank in the manuscript, and no code or data release link is provided. The system also relies on closed-source models (GPT-5-mini, Gemini-3-Flash, Grok-4.1-fast, DeepSeekV3.2), making exact replication difficult.

External evidence retrieval is not controlled for temporal contamination. Since the benchmark is built from ICLR 2023 and uses a live search API, retrieved papers may postdate the original rebuttal context, which could inflate evidence-support scores.

The benchmark scale is small for the headline challenge set (20 papers / 106 cases), and the human study is limited. Generalization across venues, review styles, and research fields remains uncertain.

Some claims are overstated, such as the framing as the 'first' multi-agent rebuttal framework, and the ablation's 'Coverage Paradox' suggests the automated coverage metric can be gamed by verbose answers, which weakens the reliability of the reported coverage gains.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored NLP application: evidence-grounded author rebuttal assistance, and reframes it from direct text generation to a decision-and-evidence organization problem.

The proposed RebuttalAgent is a clearly specified multi-agent pipeline with inspectable intermediate artifacts (concern extraction, hybrid manuscript context, external evidence bundles, response plan, checker modules) that make the reasoning process more transparent than monolithic LLM prompting.

The paper introduces RebuttalBench, a benchmark derived from public ICLR 2023 OpenReview threads, with a multidimensional rubric covering relevance/coverage, argumentation quality, and communication quality rather than surface-level text overlap.
Experimental results across four base LLMs show consistent improvements over direct-to-text baselines, and additional comparisons to RAG, AutoGen, and Jiu-Jitsu help contextualize the contribution.

The ablation study provides useful evidence about which components matter, particularly highlighting evidence construction as the most critical module and analyzing the counterintuitive coverage paradox.

An author-centric human preference study with 9 domain experts and 33 generated drafts offers external validation, with a moderate-to-strong correlation (tau = 0.646) between human judgments and the automated rubric.

The appendix includes extensive prompt templates, scoring criteria, filtering details, case studies, and limitations/ethics discussion, which substantially improves clarity and potential reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core quantitative benchmark is small (20 papers, 106 multi-turn cases) and built from public ICLR 2023 data; the paper does not discuss potential pretraining contamination, which is especially relevant when evaluating generated rebuttals to publicly available review threads.

Evaluation relies heavily on an LLM-as-judge rubric. Although human validation is provided, the correlation is moderate and the judge may still reward verbosity, generic coverage, or stylistic polish in ways that are not fully characterized beyond the coverage-paradox case study.

The human preference study, while valuable, involves only 9 evaluators assessing their own recent submissions; this limits statistical power and may introduce evaluator-specific biases. Inter-annotator agreement and broader participant diversity are not reported.

The claimed benefits of transparency, controllability, and human-in-the-loop verification are not directly measured in a user study; the main experiments run in fully automated mode, so those advantages remain partly qualitative.

Although the paper discusses SFT/direct-to-text approaches as flawed, the main empirical comparison is against prompted LLMs rather than a trained rebuttal-generation model, leaving some claimed advantages less strongly demonstrated.

The paper states that code/artifacts will be available via a project page/demo, but no explicit reproducibility statement or accessible link is evident in the manuscript images; full replication of the multi-agent pipeline and benchmark construction would require substantial engineering details.

External evidence retrieval is central to the method, yet citation accuracy, retrieval precision, and potential propagation of unsupported references are not quantified systematically beyond illustrative case studies.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: assisting authors with evidence-based rebuttal writing, a high-stakes stage of the peer-review process.
The paper is clearly organized and the proposed RebuttalAgent pipeline decomposes rebuttal generation into inspectable stages: concern extraction, evidence construction, plan checking, and drafting.
The authors introduce RebuttalBench and attempt multidimensional evaluation beyond surface-level text overlap, including coverage, argumentation, and communication quality.
The manuscript provides detailed prompt templates, rubrics, ablation experiments, and qualitative case studies, which improves transparency of the proposed workflow.
The idea of separating interpretive defense from necessary experimental intervention and using action items instead of fabricating results is sensible and responsible.
weaknesses: The benchmark construction is not a reliable ground-truth signal for rebuttal quality: labels are derived from reviewer follow-up reactions (e.g., resolved/unresolved), which may reflect acceptance outcomes, reviewer mood, or paper strength rather than the quality of the rebuttal itself.

The central evaluation relies on an LLM-as-judge rubric, defaulting to Gemini-3-Flash. This introduces potential self-preference bias and prompt sensitivity, and the rubric is not validated at sufficient scale.

The human preference study is limited: only 9 authors and 33 generated drafts, with a Kendall tau of 0.646. This is a moderate correlation and not strong enough to establish the automated metric as a trustworthy proxy.

Reproducibility is weak. The paper depends on proprietary and versioned closed-source models, leaves the project page/HF demo blank, and does not release code, data, or evaluation artifacts. Prompt templates alone do not enable reproduction.

The multi-agent framework is largely an engineering composition of existing prompting strategies and tool calls, with no substantial algorithmic or theoretical novelty. The claim of being the 'first multi-agents framework' is not adequately supported.
The main results show only modest improvements over direct-to-text baselines on the proposed automated metrics, and no statistical significance tests are reported.

The ablation study reveals that removing checker modules can increase the automated Coverage score, which suggests the metric may reward verbose over-generation and can be gamed. The authors explain this away with a qualitative case study, but it undermines confidence in the headline metric.

The system generates action items and placeholders rather than actual experimental evidence, but the evaluation rubric rewards evidence-backed responses. This creates a mismatch between what the system can produce and what the metric claims to measure.

The direct-to-text baselines may be under-optimized: using a single generic prompt is a weak comparison for current LLM capabilities, and the claimed gains may partly reflect prompt engineering rather than a robust methodological advance.
Practical costs and latency of the multi-agent pipeline are not evaluated, despite being a likely barrier to real-world use.
